title: In Historic First, Pope Apologizes for Vatican's Role in Legitimizing Slavery
summary: Pope Leo XIV made history on Monday by issuing the first-ever papal apology for the Vatican's direct role in legitimizing slavery. In his inaugural encyclical, "Magnifica Humanitas," the U.S.-born pontiff expressed "deep sorrow" for the "immense suffering" caused by 15th-century papal bulls that gave European sovereigns authority to subjugate and enslave non-Christians. He called the Church's record a "wound in Christian memory." The apology specifically references documents like the 1452 bull Dum Diversas, in which Pope Nicholas V granted Portugal's king the right "to invade, conquer, fight and subjugate" and to "reduce their persons to perpetual slavery." Subsequent popes confirmed these permissions, forming the basis of the Doctrine of Discovery that legitimized colonial-era land seizures. While the Vatican formally repudiated that doctrine in 2023, it never rescinded the bulls themselves. Leo acknowledged that it's impossible to judge historical morality by today's standards, but added: "Yet neither can we deny or diminish the delay with which both society and the church came to denounce the scourge of slavery." He noted that his namesake, Pope Leo XIII, was the first pope to explicitly condemn slavery — in 1888, long after many nations had abolished it. The apology was welcomed by Black Catholic scholars. Historian Shannen Dee Williams called it a "monumental step toward essential truth-telling and reparation." She said, "The Catholic Church has never been an innocent bystander in the history of white supremacy." Leo, whose own ancestry includes both enslaved people and slaveholders, tied the historical wrong to modern concerns, warning that the digital revolution is fueling "new forms of slavery and colonialism."
why_it_matters: When a centuries-old global institution like the Catholic Church admits a grave historical wrong, it reshapes how millions of people understand guilt, responsibility and the possibility of repair. For young people, the apology raises questions about how collective memory works, what meaningful reparation looks like, and why it can take so long for powerful institutions to face uncomfortable truths.

background_read: Pope Leo XIV (the first U.S.-born leader of the worldwide Catholic Church) issued the apology in his inaugural encyclical, a document that sets the tone for his papacy. The apology directly confronts 15th-century papal bulls—official decrees sealed with a lead seal—that gave European rulers religious permission to invade non-Christian lands and enslave their inhabitants.

The bull Dum Diversas (1452), issued by Pope Nicholas V (the head of the church at the time), explicitly authorised Portugal’s King Alfonso V ‘to invade, conquer, fight and subjugate’ and ‘reduce their persons to perpetual slavery.’ Later popes confirmed these permissions, and they became the basis of the Doctrine of Discovery, a legal and theological concept that treated non-Christian lands as open for European takeover.

The Vatican formally repudiated the doctrine only in 2023 but did not rescind the bulls themselves. Pope Leo XIV acknowledged that while we cannot judge the past by today’s standards alone, the church’s slowness to condemn slavery was a failure. He noted that his namesake, Pope Leo XIII, did not condemn the slave trade until 1888—centuries after the first bulls.

Black Catholic historian Shannen Dee Williams (a leading scholar on the Black Catholic experience) called the apology a monumental step but emphasised that the Church was never an innocent bystander in white supremacy. The Pope’s own ancestry includes both enslaved people and slaveholders, giving his words a personal dimension. The encyclical also warned that new digital technologies risk creating modern forms of slavery and colonialism.

perspectives.description: Many see the apology as a long-overdue moral reckoning that validates the suffering of millions of enslaved people and their descendants. By naming specific documents and linking them to the Doctrine of Discovery, the Pope sets a precedent for other institutions to examine their own histories honestly. Black Catholic scholars hope this opens the door to concrete reparation and educational efforts.

Critics argue that an apology without material compensation or without rescinding the actual bulls is more symbolic than substantive. Some point out that the Church only issued the apology in 2026, more than 500 years after Dum Diversas, and that its tax-exempt wealth and global influence could have been used far earlier to right these wrongs. Sceptics also worry the apology might be used to deflect calls for direct financial reparations.

Historians note that the slow pace of institutional apology reflects how powerful bodies manage memory and legitimacy. The gap between the 2023 repudiation of the Doctrine of Discovery and this apology shows a pattern of iterative but incomplete accountability. The encyclical’s link to modern digital slavery also suggests a strategic move to frame the issue as eternal vigilance rather than only a one-time historical debt.

The apology could lead to formal rescission of Dum Diversas and related bulls, the creation of a truth commission on the Church’s colonial legacy, or reparations funds. It may also influence ongoing international conversations about restitution for slavery and colonialism, putting pressure on other governments and institutions. For the faithful, it could reshape church teaching on justice and spur educational reforms in Catholic schools worldwide.
